The ending feels completely natural and earned because it brings the central emotional arc and thematic motifs of the story to a poignant resolution. Throughout the second half of the story, the narrator realizes that the mother had preserved the "remnants" of the previous visit—the unmoved mug, the open book, the turned photograph, and the rationed jam—as a way to keep the visit alive in her loneliness and declining health. When the narrator breaks a twenty-year habit and intentionally leaves the dirty dishes in the sink before driving away, it is a purposeful act built directly on this realization, deliberately leaving behind new remnants for the mother to hold onto. Furthermore, framing the ending with the drive back mirrors the opening of the story, providing a strong sense of structural closure.
